as_told: An early computer translation system was given the Bible saying "The spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak" to put into Russian. When the Russian was translated back into English, it came out as "The vodka is good, but the meat is rotten." The story is told to show that machine translation cannot handle idioms or meaning.
lesson: Machine translation that works word by word, without understanding, produces wrong and absurd output.
what_happened: The earliest machine version I found was printed in February 1958 in The Linguists' Review, at the end of A.G. Readett's account of a lecture on machine translation, under the heading 'Apocryphal'. In it an unnamed firm's 'electronic brain' turns the saying into Russian, and a linguist reads it back as 'the whisky is agreeable but the meat has gone bad'. Two years earlier, in April 1956, E.H. Ullrich joked in a discussion at the Institution of Electrical Engineers about press translations such as 'the ghost wills but the meat is feeble'. In 1995 the historian of machine translation John Hutchins found no evidence that any system of the kind described existed, and noted that American work translated from Russian, not into it. I found no record of a real system output with these words.
false_part: No known machine translation system produced this output; the earliest machine version was printed as a joke labelled 'Apocryphal'.

earliest_telling.where: The Linguists' Review, NS vol. 1 pt. 2, pp. 27-28, as reprinted in John Hutchins, "The whisky was invisible", or Persistent myths of MT, MT News International 11 (June 1995)
earliest_telling.quote: A Firm experimenting with an electronic brain designed to translate English into Russian fed it with the words: "The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak."

original.what: The punch line of the 1958 telling, as reprinted by Hutchins in 1995 (the 1958 journal is not online)
original.quote: that the whisky is agreeable but the meat has gone bad

original.what: E.H. Ullrich's remark in the discussion after a lecture at the Institution of Electrical Engineers, April 1956, about poor press translation by humans, as reprinted by Hutchins in 1995
original.quote: the ghost wills but the meat is feeble

lesson_verdict.why: The 1966 report of the U.S. National Academy of Sciences committee on machine translation found that unedited machine output was sometimes misleading and sometimes wrong, and that useful machine translation was not in prospect. This supports the lesson for the systems of that time, though it does not show this particular error.

source.what: Automatic Language Processing Advisory Committee (ALPAC), Language and Machines: Computers in Translation and Linguistics, National Academy of Sciences, National Research Council, Washington, D.C., 1966
source.quote: Unedited machine output from scientific text is decipherable for the most part, but it is sometimes misleading and sometimes wrong

search_steps: Saved John Hutchins, "The whisky was invisible", or Persistent myths of MT (MT News International 11, June 1995) from hutchinsweb.me.uk. It traces the story to Readett 1958 and Ullrich 1956, and cites Kouwenhoven in Harper's Magazine, August 1962.
Open Library full-text search for "vodka is good but the meat": earliest dated hit 1974 (White tie tales), a human-interpreter version; no hit from the 1950s.

Open Library full-text search for "flesh is weak" "translating machine": hits include Kouwenhoven's collection Half a truth is better than none (undated in index), and books from 1964 on; the Kouwenhoven book on archive.org is restricted (HTTP 401 for its text).
Open Library full-text search for "flesh is weak" "electronic brain" Russian: earliest relevant hit 1967 (The Bedside Book of Laughter).
Two other Open Library queries ("spirit is willing" with vodka or meat) returned no hits.
Checked early machine translation papers in the mt-archive on aclanthology.org (Booth 1958, Delavenay 1960, Bar-Hillel 1959, IBM 1960, Reynolds 1956, Schweisheimer 1955): none contains the saying.
Papers Past (blocked by a bot check) and Chronicling America (HTTP 403) could not be searched. Snopes returned HTTP 402.
The Linguists' Review 1958 and the 1956 IEE Proceedings discussion are not online in full text; not obtained.
For the lesson, saved the 1966 ALPAC report from the mt-archive on aclanthology.org.
confidence_note: I could not read any telling from the 1950s directly. The 1956 and 1958 quotes come from Hutchins's 1995 article, which reprints them; Hutchins is a debunker, and I use him only as the reprint of those texts. An earlier telling may exist in newspapers that I could not search.
